title: The Adani Saga in America Is Over. The Bill: $275 Million, Zero Convictions, and a $10 Billion Pledge.
excerpt: The DOJ has dropped all charges with prejudice, the SEC has settled, and OFAC has its money — leaving India's most controversial conglomerate free to pursue its vast American ambitions
body:
On 18 May, a federal court in the Eastern District of New York signed an order that Indian markets had been waiting for since late 2024: the criminal indictment against Gautam Adani and his nephew Sagar Adani was dismissed with prejudice. In legal terms, it is the most definitive outcome a defendant can hope for — the charges cannot be refiled on the same facts. The most consequential American legal reckoning an Indian conglomerate has ever faced is formally closed.

The Department of Justice cited prosecutorial discretion. "The Department of Justice has reviewed this case and has decided, in its prosecutorial discretion, not to devote further resources to these criminal charges," it stated. The defence had argued throughout that no credible evidence supported the alleged bribery scheme, that the SEC lacked jurisdiction over both men, and that none of the Adani Group's entities had been charged under the Foreign Corrupt Practices Act.

## The Settlement Ledger

The DOJ dismissal is the capstone of a broader set of closures. The Securities and Exchange Commission settled its civil lawsuit against Gautam Adani last week, with the billionaire and Sagar Adani paying $6 million and $12 million respectively. Then, on Monday, the Treasury Department's Office of Foreign Assets Control announced the headline number: a $275 million civil settlement with Adani Enterprises Limited over apparent violations of US sanctions on Iran.

The OFAC case rested on 32 shipments of liquefied petroleum gas that Adani Enterprises purchased from a Dubai-based trader between November 2023 and June 2025. The trader claimed the gas originated in Oman and Iraq; OFAC determined it came from Iran. The payments — totalling approximately $192 million, all processed through US financial institutions — triggered American jurisdiction. The original statutory penalty could have reached $384 million; Adani's cooperation during the investigation reduced it to $275 million.

## The Art of the Exit

The Adani Group has consistently denied all allegations. It pointed out that none of its entities faced charges under the FCPA, and that Adani Green Energy — the renewable-energy arm at the centre of the original fundraising allegations — was never formally a party to the proceedings. Whether by legal strategy, diplomatic pressure, or the sheer impracticality of prosecuting an Indian conglomerate in an American court, the outcome is unambiguous: no conviction, no admission of guilt, and a financial penalty that, while substantial, represents roughly two weeks of the group's consolidated revenue.

Gautam Adani has pledged to invest $10 billion in the American economy — a figure that dwarfs the combined settlements and penalties. Sceptics will note the timing. But the promise signals that Adani's US ambitions, which span ports, data centres, and defence manufacturing, are expanding rather than retreating.

## What It Means for Indian Markets

For NRI investors holding Adani stocks and bonds, the resolution removes the single largest regulatory overhang since the Hindenburg Research report of January 2023. Adani Group shares had already begun recovering in anticipation of the settlement, but the "with prejudice" dismissal carries a psychological weight that no financial settlement alone could deliver.

The broader signal for Indian conglomerates is ambivalent. On one hand, the Adani outcome demonstrates that US regulatory entanglements — however alarming — can be navigated and closed. On the other, the $275 million OFAC penalty and the underlying facts about Iranian LPG procurement raise governance questions that Indian regulators and minority shareholders may yet choose to examine.

## The Road Ahead

SEBI chairman Tuhin Kanta Pandey said this week that Indian markets remain resilient to geopolitical shocks. The Adani resolution tests that thesis in miniature: a year and a half of American legal uncertainty, absorbed and processed by a market that has learned to price in volatility.

For the diaspora investor class, the lesson is characteristically Indian in its duality. The system works — charges were investigated, arguments were heard, settlements were reached. And the system bends — $275 million is a rounding error for a conglomerate whose founder remains one of the world's ten richest people. Whether that inspires confidence or unease depends entirely on which side of the ledger you read first.
